candidates.headline: The single-element argument that Δ′≈Δ does not imply the same holds when the search scales every channel
candidates.claim: The error-reduction derivation relies on the claim that scaling one weight rarely changes the group maximum. The search space s = s_X^α assigns a scale to every input channel, so many weights per group are scaled at once. The derivation's guarantee therefore does not transfer directly to the deployed search. Quality in that regime rests on the output-level search objective rather than on the analytic argument.
candidates.paper_fact: Scaling up a single element w usually does not change the maximum value from the group w.
candidates.premise: With absmax quantization, the step size Δ follows the maximum magnitude in a group. If several weights in the same group are scaled up, the group maximum is more likely to grow. Δ′ then exceeds Δ, which cancels part of the 1/s benefit, and for non-salient weights it increases error.
candidates.inference: Table 2 only varies the 1% salient channels, where Δ′≠Δ in 2.8–21.2% of groups. The final method scales all channels by activation magnitude raised to α. Δ′/Δ in that regime is not reported, and neither is how far the Eq. 3 argument holds there. The α grid search against the layer output error (Eq. 4) can absorb this effect, but the analytic justification does not cover it.
candidates.toy_example: Illustration only, not a measurement: a group with weights [1.0, 0.5, 0.4, 0.3]. Scaling only the second weight by 2 keeps the max at 1.0, so Δ′=Δ. Scaling the second weight by 4 gives a max of 2.0 and Δ′=2Δ. Scaling all four by 2 gives Δ′=2Δ, so the relative error ratio Δ′/Δ·1/s is 1 and no gain remains.
candidates.conditional_consequence: As the fraction of scaled channels per group rises, the Δ′≈Δ assumption weakens and the gain bound from Eq. 3 shrinks. The observed result then depends on the empirical α search.
candidates.critical_link: The group-maximum invariance holds for one or few scaled elements but not necessarily for the all-channel scale used by the α search.
necessary_conditions: The scaled channels do not dominate the group max, or the scale spread within a group is modest.
The absmax group quantizer is used.
defeaters: The α grid search selects a scale at which Δ′/Δ stays near 1.
Scales within a group are nearly uniform, which cancels in relative terms.
do_not_infer: That AWQ's final perplexity gains are unreliable; Tables 3 and 4 report empirical gains.
That the α search fails; it is evaluated end to end.
That Δ′/Δ values for the all-channel scale were measured; the paper reports them only for the 1% salient channels.

candidates.headline: A roughly uniform rounding error does not guarantee the derived error ratio at very low bit-width
candidates.claim: The analysis treats RoundErr as uniform with mean 0.25 and Δ and x as error-free. These are empirical regularities the authors call approximations, and they plausibly weaken when few quantization levels exist, as in INT2.
candidates.paper_fact: the error is roughly uniformly distributed from [0,0.5], resulting in an average error of 0.25
candidates.premise: Uniform rounding error is a good model when weights spread over many levels. With very few levels or non-uniform weight distributions, the residual is not uniform, and RoundErr(ws/Δ') need not equal RoundErr(w/Δ).
candidates.inference: The cancellation RoundErr(ws/Δ') ≈ RoundErr(w/Δ) is only a heuristic. It is least secure in the INT2 setting, where the paper reports RTN fails and AWQ needs GPTQ added.
candidates.toy_example: Illustration only, not a measurement: with 2-bit levels {-2,-1,0,1} and a weight that sits near a rounding boundary, scaling by s can move it from error 0.05 to 0.45 in units of Δ, so the expected error is not preserved for that element.
candidates.conditional_consequence: If rounding error after scaling is not on average equal to that before, the 1/s gain in the relative error is overstated or understated for individual groups.
candidates.critical_link: The empirical uniform-rounding assumption versus the low-level, non-uniform weights of INT2 quantization.
necessary_conditions: Weights are spread over many quantization levels
Group sizes are large enough for the empirical distribution to apply
defeaters: INT2 or very small groups
Sparse or heavy-tailed weight groups
do_not_infer: Do not infer that the INT2 failure is caused by this assumption alone
Do not infer that INT3/INT4 results are unreliable, since those are measured directly
The paper does not test the assumption at INT2

candidates.headline: Absence of calibration overfitting does not imply Pile text calibration covers image-conditioned activation statistics
candidates.claim: The paper argues that because AWQ uses no reconstruction or backpropagation, it applies directly to VLMs. That argument does not show that per-channel activation scales measured on text-only calibration data match the activation magnitudes the language tower sees when image tokens are in context.
candidates.paper_fact: Since our method does not have the overfitting issue to the calibration set, it can be directly applied to VLMs
candidates.premise: AWQ's scales come from the per-channel average activation magnitude s_X. Image-token embeddings come from a vision encoder and projector, so their per-channel magnitudes can differ in distribution from text-token activations. Avoiding regression-style overfitting limits how much the method fits to the calibration set, but it does not make the measured statistics modality-invariant.
candidates.inference: If the VLM language tower is calibrated on Pile text (the paper states Pile calibration for AWQ in general but does not say what calibration data was used for the VLMs), channels that are salient only under image-token inputs may get too little scaling. The paper's robustness evidence (PubMed vs Enron) covers only shifts between text domains, so it does not test this case.
candidates.toy_example: Not a measurement: suppose channel 17 has mean |x| of 0.1 on text but 5.0 on image tokens. A text-derived scale treats it as non-salient, and with s = s_X^alpha its weights get almost no protection exactly where image-conditioned inputs depend on it.
candidates.conditional_consequence: If image-token activations have outlier or salient channels that are absent in text, Pile-calibrated scales under-protect them. Degradation would then be larger on vision-heavy tasks than the text-only perplexity robustness results suggest.
candidates.critical_link: Whether the salient-channel ranking by mean activation magnitude is the same for image-conditioned and text-only inputs in the language tower.
necessary_conditions: VLM calibration used text-only data, or data without image tokens
Image-token activations have a different channel-magnitude profile from text tokens
The benchmark depends enough on image-token pathways to expose the mismatch
defeaters: Calibration for the VLMs actually included image-conditioned inputs
Salient channels in the language tower are largely modality-independent
Group-wise INT4 error is small enough that scale misallocation does not matter (VILA results are close to FP16)
do_not_infer: That AWQ fails on VLMs: Tables 6 and 7 show small degradation at INT4
That the authors calibrated VLMs on text only: the excerpt does not state this
That the vision encoder's activations matter, since it is not quantized

candidates.headline: Orthogonality to GPTQ does not imply that AWQ's calibration-robustness advantage survives in the combined pipeline
candidates.claim: Table 9 shows that AWQ+GPTQ lowers INT2 WikiText-2 perplexity compared with GPTQ alone. This does not show that the combination keeps AWQ's cross-domain robustness. The paper credits that robustness to AWQ using no reconstruction, but the combined pipeline includes GPTQ's reconstruction step. The paper never tests the combination on shifted calibration or evaluation distributions.
candidates.paper_fact: AWQ does not rely on any backpropagation or reconstruction
candidates.premise: GPTQ fits quantized weights to calibration activations by layer-wise reconstruction. A pipeline that includes such a step inherits some exposure to the calibration distribution, whatever preprocessing precedes it.
candidates.inference: AWQ's robustness argument depends on the absence of reconstruction. Once GPTQ reconstruction runs after AWQ scaling, that argument no longer applies. The robustness of the combined INT2 model is therefore untested rather than inherited. The paper's robustness experiment (Fig. 8) covers only AWQ versus GPTQ at INT3-g128 on OPT-6.7B.
candidates.toy_example: Not a measurement: suppose the calibration set is emails and the evaluation set is biomedical abstracts. The combined model could score well on WikiText-2 yet degrade on the abstracts like GPTQ does, because the reconstruction step fits email activations.
candidates.conditional_consequence: If the GPTQ stage of the combination overfits the calibration set, then the combined INT2 model would show a larger cross-domain perplexity gap than AWQ alone. The Table 9 gains would then be in-distribution gains only.
candidates.critical_link: Whether GPTQ reconstruction applied after AWQ scaling reintroduces calibration-set overfitting measurable under distribution shift.
necessary_conditions: The combined pipeline runs the full GPTQ reconstruction after AWQ scaling.
Calibration and evaluation distributions differ.
GPTQ's overfitting at INT3 carries over to INT2-g64.
defeaters: AWQ scaling may reduce the reconstruction error GPTQ must fit, which would reduce overfitting.
The overfitting gap may shrink at INT2 because quantization noise dominates.

candidates.headline: Orthogonality to GPTQ conflicts with an unexplained, non-monotonic gain across model scale
candidates.claim: The paper offers 'orthogonal to GPTQ' as the explanation for the INT2 gains. It gives no mechanism for why AWQ helps on top of GPTQ. The gain pattern across OPT sizes is not what a simple additive effect would produce.
candidates.paper_fact: Our method is orthogonal to GPTQ.
candidates.premise: If two independent corrections each remove a separate error source, the combined benefit would usually vary smoothly with model size. A non-monotonic pattern suggests interaction or noise, which orthogonality does not explain.

Each cell appears to be a single run, so seed variance is also unreported.

candidates.headline: Per-channel activation saliency does not guarantee that salient channels are protected within their group-128 quantization scale
candidates.claim: M1 ranks input channels by mean activation magnitude, but quantization error is set per group of 128 weights by that group's absolute maximum. How much a salient channel gains from protection therefore depends on which group it falls in and on how its scaling moves the group scale. The ranking alone does not fix this.
candidates.paper_fact: Scaling up a single element w usually does not change the maximum value from the group w.
candidates.premise: In group-wise quantization, every weight in a group shares one step size, set by the largest magnitude in that group. A channel-level importance ranking does not see group membership.
candidates.inference: The paper's assumption that the step size stays unchanged (Delta' ~ Delta) is only approximate. Table 2 shows the share of changed Delta rising with s (2.8% to 21.2%). So the protection a salient channel receives, and the damage to its non-salient group neighbours, depends on how salient channels are spread across groups, not only on the channel ranking.
candidates.toy_example: Not a measurement: if two salient channels share one group and are both scaled up, they can raise that group's maximum, which coarsens the step size for its non-salient neighbours. If the same two channels sit in separate groups, each group is affected less.
candidates.conditional_consequence: If salient channels cluster inside a few groups, or sit next to large-weight neighbours, then the same channel ranking can give a smaller error reduction than the paper's average statistics suggest.
candidates.critical_link: Channel-level activation ranking -> group-level shared step size, with the assumption Delta' ~ Delta holding only on average.
necessary_conditions: Salient channels share groups with non-salient channels
The scaling step (M2) enlarges the group maximum for at least some groups
The number of such groups is large enough to affect output error
defeaters: Salient channels spread evenly across groups
Scale factors small enough (s <= 2) that Delta rarely changes
Per-layer search over alpha absorbs the effect, since it measures output error directly
do_not_infer: Do not infer that AWQ fails at group size 128.
Do not infer a measured per-group error breakdown; the paper reports none.
Do not infer that the FP16-retention results in Table 1 suffer from this mismatch in the same way, because those channels skip quantization entirely.

candidates.headline: An equivalent per-channel scaling does not guarantee hardware-friendliness when s^-1 cannot be fused into a preceding operator
candidates.claim: The mechanism avoids a mixed FP16/INT4 format by moving the compensation s^-1 onto the activations. The paper supports hardware-friendliness only through the statement that this inverse scale 'can usually' be fused. For input channels with no fusable predecessor, the hardware benefit is not established by the paper.
candidates.paper_fact: for s−1 · X, it can usually be fused into the previous
candidates.premise: A scale on the input activations of a linear layer is free only if some earlier operator (for example a norm layer or a linear layer's output) can absorb it into its own parameters. Otherwise it is a separate elementwise multiply executed at inference time.
candidates.inference: Where no such operator exists, the equivalent transformation still keeps a uniform low-bit weight format but adds runtime work and a kernel launch. The paper's argument for hardware-friendliness over mixed precision then weakens for those layers. The text does not say which layers or architectures fall into this case.
candidates.toy_example: Illustration only, not a measurement: a layer whose input comes from an operator that cannot absorb a per-channel scale. It needs one extra elementwise multiply of hidden-dimension size per token, which is a memory-bound op that is small in FLOPs but costs a launch.
candidates.conditional_consequence: If s^-1 cannot be folded, the cost moves from mixed-precision kernel complexity to extra per-token operators. The hardware-friendly claim holds only to the extent that fusion is available.
candidates.critical_link: Whether the layer's input is produced by an operator that can absorb a per-channel scale.
necessary_conditions: A preceding operator exists whose parameters can absorb s^-1.
The scaled input channels all pass through that operator.
defeaters: Layers whose inputs come from non-parametric or shared ops with no absorbable scale.
Architectures where several consumers share one producer but need different scales.
do_not_infer: That AWQ is slower than FP16 in general.
That fusion fails in the reported models; the paper measures speedups on them.
That the quantization quality is affected by the fusion issue.

candidates.headline: A smaller per-element relative error for a scaled salient weight does not imply lower layer output error
candidates.claim: The closed-form ratio (Δ'/Δ)·(1/s) describes the relative rounding error of one scaled weight element. By itself it does not predict whether the output error of the layer or model falls, because output error also depends on the other elements in the group and on how Δ moves.
candidates.paper_fact: Given ∆ ′ ≈∆and s > 1, the relative error is smaller for the salient weight w.
candidates.premise: In absmax group quantization, Δ is shared by every element in a group. Any change in Δ changes the rounding error of all those elements, and output error sums contributions across elements and channels.
candidates.inference: The ratio 1/s is a motivating quantity for one element under Δ'≈Δ. A monotone benefit in s for the whole network does not follow from it. The paper itself says non-salient channels must be considered separately.
candidates.toy_example: Illustration only, not a measurement: a group has one salient element and 127 others. Scaling the salient element by s=4 halves its relative error twice over, but if that raises Δ by 20%, the 127 others each get about 20% more absolute error. The sum can then rise.
candidates.conditional_consequence: If Δ' grows noticeably with s, the net output error can stop improving or get worse, even though the salient element's relative error keeps falling.
candidates.critical_link: Relative error of a single element versus the output-level objective L(s) over all elements in the group.
necessary_conditions: Δ' ≈ Δ holds for most groups
Non-salient elements contribute little extra error
defeaters: Δ changes in many groups as s grows
Non-salient channels carry non-trivial activation magnitude
do_not_infer: Do not infer that the scaling idea is wrong
Do not infer that the grid-searched α fails, since it optimizes the output objective directly

candidates.headline: The assumption that the maximum is unchanged conflicts with scaling many channels in the same group
candidates.claim: The Δ'≈Δ step is justified for scaling a single element. In practice about 1% of input channels are scaled together, so a group can contain several scaled elements. Table 2 shows that the share of groups with changed Δ rises quickly with s.
candidates.paper_fact: Scaling up a single element w usually does not change the maximum value from the group w.
candidates.premise: A group's absmax can only stay fixed if no scaled element becomes the new maximum. The chance of a changed maximum rises with the number of scaled elements and with s.
candidates.inference: The single-element argument is an approximation that gets worse as s increases or as more channels fall in one group. The paper's own statistics (Δ changes in 8.2% of groups at s=2 and 21.2% at s=4) show this.

candidates.headline: Minimizing layer-local output error does not imply or guarantee optimal end-to-end model quality
candidates.claim: The α search is driven by a per-layer output-difference objective (Eq. 4). It never directly optimizes final perplexity or task quality, so a lower local error need not translate into a better final model.
candidates.paper_fact: we choose to automatically search for an optimal (per input channel) scaling factor that minimizes the output difference after quantization for a certain layer.
candidates.premise: Quantization errors from successive transformer layers interact and compound through the network. A per-layer objective can be minimized at every layer without minimizing the loss of the full model.
candidates.inference: The selected α is the best of 20 grid points for each layer's local error on cached calibration inputs. Nothing in the objective constrains the cross-layer accumulated error, so the final-perplexity gap is not controlled by the search. The paper's own Table 3 shows the search does not always reach the mixed-precision reference: at OPT-13B, AWQ is 10.56 against 10.43 for 1% FP16.
candidates.toy_example: Illustration only, not a measurement: suppose layer A's best local α slightly shifts its output in a direction that layer B amplifies. The local losses are both minimal, but the final logits are worse than with a slightly different α at A.
candidates.conditional_consequence: If errors compound across layers, deeper models or lower bit widths could show a larger gap between the sum of local losses and final perplexity. This is untested in the paper.
candidates.critical_link: Local layer output error is only a proxy for final perplexity, and the proxy gap is neither measured nor bounded.

The local optimum α differs from the α that is best for the downstream loss
defeaters: Local errors are small and roughly additive, so the proxy is tight

candidates.headline: A single per-layer α does not imply or guarantee the optimal scale for every channel
candidates.claim: The search fixes the scale shape to s = sX^α and tunes only one exponent per layer. Every channel is therefore forced onto a one-parameter family tied to its mean activation, even though the scale is applied per channel.
candidates.paper_fact: we use a single hyper-parameter α to balance between the protection of salient and non-salient channels.
candidates.premise: A one-dimensional family of per-channel scales is a strict subset of all per-channel scale vectors. Its optimum is generally no better than, and often worse than, the optimum over the full space.
candidates.inference: The paper's Eq. 5 restricts search to α in [0,1] with a grid size of 20. The best α is a compromise across channels with possibly different saliency and quantization-error tradeoffs. Per-channel or per-group exponents are not tested, so any gain from them is unmeasured.
candidates.conditional_consequence: If channels within a layer differ in how strongly they trade salient protection against non-salient error, a per-group α could achieve lower layer error at higher search cost. The paper does not test this.
candidates.critical_link: The scale shape is fixed by the mean-activation function, and only a layer-wide exponent is learned.

The layer's error is sensitive to that variation
defeaters: Mean activation magnitude already orders channels well enough that the single exponent is near-optimal
The weight clipping step absorbs the residual mismatch
Finer search overfits the small calibration set

candidates.headline: Clipping to minimize quantization MSE does not guarantee lower layer-output error

candidates.headline: A batch-size-1 roofline derivation of a 4× W4A16 bound does not imply or guarantee the same benefit at larger batch sizes or long prompts
candidates.claim: The case for weight-only 4-bit quantization is derived entirely in the batch-1, single-stream generation regime. The paper shows no analysis or measurement of how the benefit changes once batching or long prompts raise arithmetic intensity.
candidates.paper_fact: We adopt an inference batch size of 1, catering for edge use cases
candidates.premise: In a matrix-vector product each weight is read once per token, and with batching each weight read is reused across the batch. FLOPs per weight byte therefore grow roughly linearly with batch size, and a workload leaves the memory-bound regime once its intensity passes the device ridge point. Dequantization adds compute per weight, which is hidden behind memory time only while the kernel stays memory-bound.
candidates.inference: Above some batch size or prompt length, memory traffic stops being the bottleneck. Weight-byte savings then buy less, and dequantization compute may become exposed. The paper's 'weight access dominates' conclusion is a batch-1 statement.
candidates.toy_example: Illustration only, not a measurement. Take an idealized model that ignores activation traffic and dequantization compute. FP16 intensity is about B FLOPs/byte and W4A16 intensity is about 4B. This matches the paper's 1 and 4 at B=1. Against the 165 FLOPs/byte ridge point the paper quotes for the 4090, W4A16 would stop being memory-bound near B≈41. FP16 would stop near B≈165.
candidates.conditional_consequence: If a deployment serves batches or long prompts beyond the break-even point, the 3-4× speedups reported at batch 1 should not be expected. W4A16 could even trail an FP16 kernel if dequantization overhead is no longer hidden. This last point is an inference, not something the paper reports.
candidates.critical_link: The step from 'arithmetic intensity ≈ 1 at batch 1' to 'weight-only is the right design' assumes the workload stays memory-bound.
necessary_conditions: Batch size is 1 and generation is single-stream.
Dequantization compute fits under memory time.
Activation and KV-cache traffic stay small relative to weight traffic.
defeaters: Large batches, long prompts or speculative decoding raise arithmetic intensity.
Hardware with very low bandwidth relative to compute stays memory-bound longer.
Kernels that dequantize cheaply, for example via LUTs or tensor-core-friendly layouts, shift the break-even point.

Do not infer that W4A16 is slower than FP16 at any particular batch size; the paper does not measure this.
Do not infer that the paper claims the 4× bound holds beyond batch 1.

candidates.headline: Fusing dequantization to avoid DRAM writes does not guarantee a net kernel speedup

candidates.toy_example: Illustration only, not a measurement: if a tile needs 10 time units of ALU work after fusion but only 6 units of memory time, latency is set by the ALU and the byte savings are not visible.
candidates.conditional_consequence: If ALU or SIMD throughput, not DRAM bandwidth, limits the kernel, the fused dequantization kernel will not deliver the bandwidth-derived speedup, and could be slower than a baseline with a cheaper dequantization path.

candidates.headline: The stated general SIMD-width rule does not guarantee a ready packing for other widths or for INT3
candidates.claim: The paper gives a rule for choosing the index offset for any 2^n-bit register. candidates.headline: Launch-overhead savings from kernel fusion at batch size 1 do not guarantee similar gains at larger batches or on slower kernels
candidates.claim: The paper's justification for fusion is that individual FP16 kernels on the 4090 take about 0.01 ms, comparable to launch overhead, in a batch-1 decode benchmark. That justification is specific to this regime, and the same fusion should help less once per-kernel compute time grows.
candidates.paper_fact: Notably, the computation time for each FP16 kernel is in the order of 0.01ms on the 4090 GPU, comparable to the GPU kernel launch overhead. Hence, reducing number of kernel calls through kernel fusion leads to direct speedups.
candidates.premise: Launch overhead is roughly a fixed cost per kernel call, while kernel runtime grows with work. Larger batches or slower devices raise runtime and shrink the launch-overhead fraction. CUDA graphs or similar runtimes can also remove launch cost without fusing kernels.
candidates.inference: Fusion's relative benefit is largest when kernel runtime is close to launch latency, which holds for tiny batch-1 kernels on a fast GPU. Outside that regime the savings are a smaller share of total latency, so the 1.2x Llama-2-7B fusion gain should not be assumed to transfer.
candidates.toy_example: Illustrative only, not a measurement: with a fixed 0.01 ms launch cost, a 0.01 ms kernel spends half its time launching. A 0.1 ms kernel spends under 10% of its time launching, so removing launches gives a much smaller gain.
candidates.conditional_consequence: If the workload moves to batched serving or the kernels become longer, the fusion share of the reported speedup would decrease. A baseline with CUDA graphs would also reduce it.
candidates.critical_link: The paper's quantitative argument for fusion is tied to the 0.01 ms kernel time on the 4090 and to the batch-1 protocol. Neither is shown to hold elsewhere.

The baseline pays per-kernel launch costs without graph capture or equivalent.
Decode is run at small batch size.
defeaters: Quantized matmuls get faster, so non-matmul overhead becomes a larger fraction and fusion's value can rise even at the same batch size.
Fusion also removes intermediate DRAM traffic, which helps independently of launch overhead.
